description.text: Giovanni Francesco Albani, later Pope Clement XI, was born on 23 July 1649 in Urbino to a family of Albanian origin that had settled in central Italy. Educated at the Collegio Romano, he earned doctorates in canon and civil law and became a respected Latinist before being made a cardinal by Pope Alexander VIII in 1690. After a decade as a papal prelate and governor of several Italian cities, he was elected pope on 23 November 1700, a rapid ascent that followed his ordination as a priest only a few months earlier.

During his pontificate he pursued a wide range of cultural and theological initiatives: he expanded the Vatican Library with Syriac manuscripts, sponsored the first public observatory in Italy, and commissioned the Illyricum Sacrum, a monumental work on the Balkans. Politically he navigated the War of the Spanish Succession, issued the controversial bull Unigenitus against Jansenism, and imposed restrictions on the Chinese Rites, declaring them idolatrous. He died in Rome on 19 March 1721 and was buried in the pavement of Saint Peter’s Basilica.

curiosities.text: He authorized excavations of the Roman catacombs, which helped preserve much of Rome’s early Christian heritage.
He commissioned the Illyricum Sacrum, a 5,000‑page Jesuit work by Daniele Farlati and Dom Jacopo Coleti that remains a key source on the medieval Balkans.
In 1720 he named Saint Anselm of Canterbury a Doctor of the Church, bestowing upon him the titles “Doctor magnificus” and “Doctor Marianus.”
